parsed_answer.content:
Developers frequently experience a cognitive dissonance when encountering a Memory Leak in Java because of the implicit trust placed in the Garbage Collector (GC). Unlike languages like C or C++ where memory must be explicitly deallocated via free or delete, the JVM handles object lifecycle management automatically through reachability analysis in the heap. However, a Java memory leak does not stem from unreleased hardware memory; rather, it is a logical leak caused by unintended object retention. An object becomes a memory leak when it is no longer needed by the business application, but remains strongly reachable from a GC root through a chain of active references. Because the garbage collector treats these objects as reachable, it cannot reclaim their memory, eventually culminating in a devastating java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

Understanding why this happens requires a deep look into the generational memory architecture of the JVM. When references are inadvertently leaked, these unwanted objects are promoted out of the Eden space through survivor spaces and eventually settle into the Tenured (Old) Generation. Because the Old Generation is collected much less frequently than the Young Generation—often requiring a full stop-the-world major GC—leaked objects quietly accumulate, consuming precious heap capacity, increasing GC pause frequencies, and drastically degrading throughput. Addressing memory leaks requires a combination of heap dump analysis (using tools like Eclipse MAT or Java Mission Control), profiling GC logs, and meticulously auditing reference chains to ensure that object lifecycles are tightly scoped and cleaned up when no longer required.

Failing to invoke free() causing physical memory loss.
Retaining strong references in collections or static fields, causing logical retention.
Heap Dumps (HPROF), VisualVM, Eclipse MAT, Flight Recorder

items: Static Field Accumulation: Storing objects in static collections (e.g., public static List) ties their lifecycle directly to the ClassLoader, meaning they live as long as the application runs unless explicitly removed.
Unclosed Resource Handles: Failing to close database connections, streams, or JDBC statements leaves internal driver references dangling in connection pools or finalizer queues.

Improper hashCode() and equals(): Using mutable objects as keys in HashMaps or HashSets without updating keys causes objects to become 'lost' inside buckets, making them impossible to remove while permanently occupying memory.

ThreadLocal Leaks: Storing values in ThreadLocal variables within pooled application threads (like Tomcat threads) without invoking threadLocal.remove() leaves strong references anchored to the thread, leaking memory across requests.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap occurs when using inner classes. Non-static inner classes (including anonymous inner classes and standard lambdas that capture outer state) maintain a hidden, synthetic strong reference to their enclosing outer class instance. If you pass an anonymous Runnable or a listener bound to a non-static inner class into a long-lived service or event bus, you instantly leak the entire outer class—often an Activity, Controller, or large Service instance—along with all the heavy dependencies it holds.

title: What is a Memory Leak in Java if Java has a Garbage Collector?
